routes.description: Establish resurrection as a plausible cumulative explanation of the early appearances, unexpected resurrection belief, subsequent Christian expansion, and continuing visions.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the historical lines jointly fit Jesus's resurrection and continuing agency more specifically than the proposed ordinary or comparative explanations.

motionBridge.description: The combined historical lines must make Jesus's resurrection a plausible explanation of the motion's specified phenomena.

centralBridges.description: Early individual and group appearance traditions must provide positive evidence that Jesus was encountered alive after death.
The immediate claim of an individually resurrected Messiah must require explanation beyond available Jewish postmortem categories.
Christianity's expansion must connect specifically to the mission and continuing agency attributed to the risen Jesus.
Later cross-cultural Jesus visions must constitute an additional phenomenon consistent with his continuing activity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: No single evidential line must bear the entire case; the lines must retain cumulative relevance when considered together.
Christian appearance and vision reports must be distinguishable from proposed parallels by their attestation, unexpectedness, or cross-cultural pattern.

routes.description: Account for the appearance beliefs, resurrection interpretation, Christian expansion, and later visions without treating a physical resurrection as the probable historical explanation.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source limitations, ordinary experiential mechanisms, cultural interpretation, religious growth, and comparative cases block the resurrection inference.

motionBridge.description: The available historical evidence must remain insufficient to prefer a unique physical resurrection over ordinary or historically comparable explanations.

centralBridges.description: The appearance evidence must be constrained by indirect testimony, sparse descriptions, and uncertainty about the reported witnesses.
Experiences and apocalyptic Jewish beliefs must supply a nonresurrection route to sincere claims that Jesus had been raised.
Religious expansion and fulfilled-mission claims must not establish what happened physically to Jesus's body.
Later Jesus dreams and visions must remain explainable through phenomena also reported in other religious traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical inference must compare probabilities without assuming either that miracles are impossible or that testimony establishes them.
Standards applied to Christian testimony must also be applied to Mormon, Marian, and ancient appearance traditions.

sections.title: Early appearance testimony and comparative attestation
sections.rationale: The quality, number, and comparative force of the earliest reported witnesses form the principal evidential link between postmortem experiences and resurrection.

sections.title: Unexpected messianic claim and Jewish interpretive categories
sections.rationale: The origin of belief in an already resurrected Messiah determines whether the claim itself points beyond ordinary experience or follows from available cultural interpretation.

sections.title: Cumulative fit and historical probability
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether several converging facts can make resurrection plausible despite the methodological difficulty of inferring a singular physical event.

sections.title: Christian expansion and the worldwide mission claim
sections.rationale: Christianity's historical reach matters only if its scale or fulfillment of an attributed mission bears specifically on resurrection rather than merely recording successful belief.

sections.title: Later visions and cross-religious parallels
sections.rationale: Post-apostolic dreams and visions provide an additional proposed evidential line whose relevance depends on whether they indicate continuing agency or generic religious experience.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Early Pauline sources are used to organize a cumulative case from Jesus's crucifixion, the unexpected resurrection claim, reported appearances, and Christianity's subsequent spread.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Justin Bass to summarize his positive case, and the uninterrupted answer follows that invitation.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the pro side's cumulative framework and therefore has no earlier opposing demand to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly organizes the principal evidential lines, though it does not yet defend their conjunction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition and its constituent lines are recoverable, with plausibility rather than proof functioning as an implicit limit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents an organizing cumulative case rather than claiming that the listed facts already necessitate resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed facts can coherently form a cumulative argument, although the independence and comparative-fit bridges remain undeveloped here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Early Pauline tradition is specifically invoked, but the move mostly inventories facts without yet documenting or comparing them.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly advances the motion-level requirement that the specified historical lines jointly make resurrection plausible.

representationalCharity.rationale: This opening framework does not engage a developed opposing alternative that permits a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names crucifixion, the novel resurrection claim, appearances catalogued in 1 Corinthians 15, and later spread.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Reports concerning Paul, Peter, James, Mary Magdalene, groups of disciples, and the five hundred form an early witness tradition offered as positive evidence of Jesus's resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly asks Justin Bass to present the appearance evidence, and the sustained first-person exposition answers that request.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative appearance-witness line and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the principal named witnesses relevant to the early-appearance bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The named witness-tradition claim is clear, but the excerpt sometimes slides between reported belief and direct witness testimony.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bass acknowledges uncertainty about Mary and invites correction, but the collective evidential force exceeds the excerpt's source distinctions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple reported experiences coherently provide some positive evidence, but reported belief does not by itself establish independent direct testimony.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific persons and 1 Corinthians 15 are identified, while source independence, directness, and the five hundred remain materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable central bridge concerning early individual and group appearance traditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily presents positive testimony and does not yet assess a developed alternative interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass names Peter, James, Paul, Mary Magdalene, disciples, and the five hundred as an early appearance tradition.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Only Paul directly attests his own experience, while claims concerning Peter, James, Mary, and the five hundred depend on indirect testimony and require comparison with other religions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Bart Ehrman's assessment, and the answer is marked by his discussion of historical source evaluation and comparative religious evidence.

components.text: Whether the named appearance reports amount to sufficiently direct and reliable multiple-witness evidence.
Whether the appearance line can carry cumulative evidential weight despite source limitations.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes Paul's self-attestation from indirect reports about Peter, James, Mary, and the five hundred, contacting the decisive evidential demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly addresses the source status of the named witnesses and identifies the resulting limit on the appearance inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between direct self-report and indirect tradition is clear, and uncertainty about particular witnesses is expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move uses probabilistic language for Peter and James, admits uncertainty about the five hundred, and limits its conclusion appropriately.

charity.alternative: Peter, James, Mary, and the five hundred may preserve genuine experiences despite indirect surviving sources.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical weight still depends on the directness, independence, and descriptive content of the surviving attestations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from indirect, uneven testimony to constrained evidential force is explicit and does not deny that experiences occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply identifies concrete source differences and uncertain witnesses, with only the broader comparative-religion support left compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central source-limits bridge governing the principal early-appearance evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ehrman grants probable experiences to several named people while maintaining the decisive source limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman distinguishes Paul's own account, probable reports from Peter and James, no direct Mary testimony, and the unexplained five hundred.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Christian appearance testimony is presented as stronger than Islamic or Mormon miracle claims because it involves multiple accepted witnesses rather than one founding visionary.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion back to Justin, whose response directly contrasts the Christian witnesses with Muhammad and Joseph Smith.

components.text: Whether Christianity has enough accepted witnesses to overcome the objection that most testimony is indirect.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the source-limit objection by emphasizing four accepted experiencers and contrasting them with single-founder claims, though it does not resolve directness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it contacts multiplicity but leaves the decisive distinction between reports about witnesses and direct testimony unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The witness-count claim is clear, but eyewitness language obscures differences between accepted experiences and surviving first-person testimony.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move treats numerical multiplicity as substantially resolving a source-quality objection without qualifying dependence and independence.

charity.alternative: Indirect reports about several people need not be stronger than direct records surrounding another religious claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiplicity matters only after directness, independence, and comparable standards are established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple witnesses can improve an inference, but the move equivocates between multiple alleged experiencers and multiple independent eyewitness accounts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a concrete numerical comparison but does not establish independence, direct documentation, or the accuracy of its Mormon characterization.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central source-limits bridge, although its answer is incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the source objection only narrowly and materially understates its directness and comparability dimensions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass invokes four experiencers accepted in discussion and contrasts them with Muhammad and Joseph Smith as single visionary founders.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Mormon testimony concerning Moroni is presented as at least as directly documented and multiply attested as much New Testament appearance testimony, requiring consistent historical treatment.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating exchange identifies Ehrman through his detailed correction about Mormon witnesses and his repeated appeal to impartial historical source evaluation.

components.text: Whether Christian claims are comparatively stronger because Mormonism rests only on Joseph Smith's solitary testimony.
Whether New Testament appearance claims possess direct testimony from the named witnesses.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the comparative premise as false or incomplete, cites multiple documented Mormon witnesses, and states that consistent treatment weakens the Christian distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly targets the decisive comparative premise and explains the defeating consequence for the claimed witness advantage.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative claim, documentary distinction, and impartiality qualification are all stated in readily recoverable terms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes a bounded comparative claim that Mormon attestation is at least as direct as much Christian testimony.

charity.alternative: Christian testimony could remain stronger because its witnesses concern appearances of Jesus rather than Moroni-related objects or events.
charity.decisiveQualification: The specific pro argument relied on witness number and documentation, criteria the Mormon comparison directly contests.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the proposed comparator has multiple direct attestations while Christian figures lack surviving direct accounts, the claimed distinction is defeated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The exchange specifies multiple Mormon testimonies and missing New Testament first-person accounts, with detailed source verification compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the subsidiary consistency bridge by requiring equal treatment of Christian and Mormon testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly tests the stated numerical and documentary distinction, though it does not exhaust every possible disanalogy.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman points to several Mormon witnesses whose testimony survives and contrasts that documentation with absent testimony from Peter, James, and the five hundred.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Paul, Peter, and Mary were not expecting Jesus or a crucified Messiah to appear, unlike later believers already possessing categories for saintly appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn continues Bass's first-person defense after the Marian comparison and names the apostles whose lack of expectation grounds his distinction.

components.text: Whether comparative religious appearances undermine Christianity despite differences in prior expectation.
Whether comparative traditions are sufficiently analogous to reduce the early appearance reports' force.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes initial Jesus experiences from later religious appearances through asserted lack of expectation, contacting the comparative demand but not source directness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive comparative component, but leaves the documentary source-limit component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The unexpectedness distinction is clear, but categorical claims about what Paul, Peter, and Mary expected lack stated evidential limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated claims that the figures were in no way expecting Jesus are stronger than the supplied evidence and omit individual uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Comparative religious visions can occur unexpectedly even within a worldview that permits such appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: General worldview availability does not establish each experiencer's immediate expectation, but neither does surprise establish external appearance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Unexpectedness can distinguish experiences from expectation-driven cases, but it does not alone establish that the perceived figure appeared externally.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named initial experiencers provide specificity, yet the categorical psychological claims and comparison with Catholics are not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary comparative-distinction bridge through unexpectedness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply notices expectation as a possible disanalogy but understates the strongest comparative alternative and its qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass argues that Paul, Peter, and Mary did not expect Jesus to appear, unlike later Catholics familiar with saintly appearances.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Unexpected Marian experiences show that lack of immediate expectation neither distinguishes the Jesus experiences nor establishes that the perceived figure appeared.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker challenges Bass's familiarity with Marian literature and repeatedly advances the skeptical comparison characteristic of Ehrman's preceding position.

components.text: Whether lack of immediate expectation uniquely distinguishes early Jesus experiences from other religious visions.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests unexpectedness as a distinction by invoking surprising Marian experiences and separating perceived appearance from actual appearance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both the proposed differentiator and the inference drawn from that differentiator, though the excerpt documents the parallel only briefly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes immediate surprise, worldview availability, perceived experience, and the external-appearance conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The bounded conclusion is that unexpectedness does not establish actuality or uniqueness, not that every experience has one explanation.

charity.alternative: The first disciples lacked the specific category of a Messiah individually rising before the general resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: That interpretive novelty may require explanation but does not show that their underlying experiences were externally caused.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A counterexample involving unexpected religious experience coherently defeats the inference from surprise to unique external causation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Marian parallel is relevant and specific, though representative documentation and frequency are not developed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the subsidiary claim that Christian experiences are distinguished by unexpectedness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the specific-category distinction while preserving the decisive gap between interpretation and actuality.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman invokes unexpected Marian experiences and argues that thinking one saw a figure does not establish that the figure appeared.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Initial followers could sincerely think they saw Jesus, after which apocalyptic Jewish embodiment beliefs could convert those experiences into the claim that God raised the Messiah.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator clarifies Bass's unexpectedness argument, Ehrman explicitly accepts the premise and develops his alternative account of how the belief formed.

components.text: Whether an unexpected resurrection belief requires the resurrection itself rather than experience followed by interpretation.
Whether novelty of the resurrection claim independently supports the cumulative resurrection inference.

response.rationale: The reply grants unexpectedness, then identifies the inference's failure: sincere experiences plus apocalyptic embodiment beliefs can generate resurrection interpretation without physical resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly accepts the strongest premise, supplies an alternative route, and states the consequence for the resurrection inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: Probable experiences, unknown additional experiencers, and subsequent apocalyptic interpretation are carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges what is known and unknown and advances a possible historical route rather than claiming certainty.

charity.alternative: The individual resurrection claim was genuinely novel and not generated by prior expectation of a rising Messiah.
charity.decisiveQualification: Novel interpretation can follow unexpected experiences using broader apocalyptic embodiment beliefs without verifying a physical resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experience-to-interpretation route is explicit, internally consistent, and directly resolves why novelty need not entail the proposed cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It uses accepted experiences and a specified Jewish apocalyptic framework, while detailed evidence for the interpretive transition remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central natural-interpretation bridge needed by the con route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly grants the central unexpectedness premise and answers its strongest inference with a qualified alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman grants that Peter, Mary, and Paul thought they saw Jesus, denies prior expectation, and proposes later apocalyptic resurrection interpretation.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jewish followers had categories for exalted or disembodied survival until the final resurrection, leaving their claim that Jesus had bodily risen already as a novel development requiring explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests a quick response, and the resulting rebuttal defends Bass's established unexpectedness argument before the scheduled break.

components.text: Whether available Jewish categories adequately explain the claim that Jesus had already risen bodily.
Whether general worldview availability eliminates the novelty of the specific resurrection interpretation.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes exalted disembodied survival and final resurrection from the immediate bodily resurrection claim, challenging the proposed interpretive route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive cultural-category premise, though it does not fully exclude recombination or innovation after experiences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relevant Jewish categories and temporal distinction are clear, with the impossibility of recombination left only implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence supports novelty, but novelty alone is slightly overstated as a barrier to experiential reinterpretation.

charity.alternative: Followers could combine experiences with broader apocalyptic resurrection beliefs to form a novel claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Existing categories did not already predict an individually resurrected crucified Messiah before the final resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The category distinction supports novelty and explanatory demand, although it does not logically rule out a novel interpretation of experiences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Maccabean exaltation and final-resurrection categories are concrete support, but representativeness and interpretive flexibility remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central natural-interpretation bridge by disputing the adequacy of available categories.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly addresses broader Jewish categories while leaving the live possibility of innovative recombination underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass contrasts Maccabean heavenly survival and resurrection at the end with the Christian claim that Jesus had risen already.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historians cannot treat an alleged one-time violation of physical law as the most probable explanation merely because a few people reported it.
moves.attributionBasis: The wording restates Ehrman's explicit objection about physical laws and contrasts historical probability with the reported claims of Paul and Peter.

components.text: Whether the cumulative historical lines can make a unique violation of physical regularity the most probable explanation.
Whether reports from a few early figures provide extraordinary evidence adequate to the singular claim.

response.rationale: The reply directly applies historical probability and the rarity of the event to the cumulative and testimonial inference, while allowing a sufficiently extraordinary evidence threshold.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative-probability demand, though the base-rate formulation is asserted more than formally defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical-probability claim is clear, but describing resurrection as a violation of physical law risks conflating divine exception with contradiction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The rarity argument is forceful but allows that incredible evidence could alter the conclusion; its physical-law language slightly overstates the premise.

charity.alternative: A singular event may still be historically probable if its evidence is sufficiently discriminating and strong.
charity.decisiveQualification: The available testimony must meet that extraordinary comparative threshold rather than merely report that the event occurred.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Comparing a uniquely rare hypothesis with ordinary alternatives is coherent, though rarity cannot alone settle posterior probability without likelihoods.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed physical regularity and sparse testimony ground the argument, but the numerical or comparative likelihood bridge is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con motion bridge that history cannot prefer resurrection over ordinary explanations on this evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly includes an extraordinary-evidence exception and therefore addresses the strongest version of the opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman contrasts an unprecedented physical exception with reports attributed to Paul and Peter and conditions acceptance on incredible evidence.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Appearances are only one component of the cumulative case, and the historical evidence is presented as consistent with what would be expected if Jesus rose.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker cites Bart's published formulation directly and uses the pro side's cumulative-case language about further evidence still to come.

components.text: Whether historical rarity defeats resurrection when the observed evidence is what resurrection would predict.
Whether an ordinary interpretive route explains the appearance evidence at least as specifically.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the rarity objection by emphasizing cumulative evidence and conditional consistency, but does not compare resurrection's likelihood with the ordinary alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that reaches the primary objection but leaves the decisive comparative-probability and rival-explanation bridge unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited claim of consistency under a resurrection hypothesis is clear and expressly separated from the complete cumulative case.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully claims consistency and further cumulative relevance, not that compatibility alone proves resurrection.

charity.alternative: The same evidence may also be consistent with sincere visionary experiences and later interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conditional fit supports resurrection only if it compares favorably with live alternatives and contributes independent information.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Expected evidence under resurrection has relevance, but consistency alone does not establish comparative plausibility or answer the base-rate challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appearance evidence supplies a factual anchor, while no discriminating prediction or alternative comparison is provided in this move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly attacks the con motion-level probability conclusion, despite leaving its main comparative bridge incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately states its limited compatibility point but largely omits the strongest comparative qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass cites Ehrman's acknowledgment that the evidence would look consistent if Jesus rose and places appearances within a larger cumulative case.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical conclusions compare probabilities, making ordinary misperception more likely than a unique physical exception even if supernatural intervention is abstractly possible.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies what historians establish and repeats Ehrman's probability comparison between rare resurrection and common mistaken experience.

components.text: Whether mere consistency with resurrection is sufficient to make it historically preferable.
Whether the cumulative case supplies likelihoods capable of overcoming ordinary comparative alternatives.

response.rationale: The reply identifies compatibility as insufficient and replaces it with comparative historical probability, explaining that ordinary error remains more likely even if miracles are possible.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses the missing comparative inference and states its consequence for the claimed resurrection fit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Abstract possibility, historical probability, ordinary misperception, and unique physical exception are distinctly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative conclusion is warranted in direction, though the extreme numerical analogy is illustrative rather than established.

charity.alternative: Resurrection may predict the reported appearances and remain possible under a theistic worldview.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical preference still requires resurrection to outperform ordinary explanations after prior rarity and evidence quality are considered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between possibility, compatibility, and comparative probability is explicit and defeats the compatibility-only inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Common mistaken experience and stable physical regularity support the comparison, though the numerical odds and case-specific likelihoods are not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the con motion route's controlling comparative-probability requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants abstract supernatural possibility and focuses accurately on the strongest comparative-probability issue.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman states that historians infer by probabilities and contrasts ordinary mistaken experience with a unique physical exception even if exceptions are possible.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jesus's singular worldwide worship and divine status are presented as an extraordinary historical anomaly that makes the further extraordinary claim of resurrection more plausible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the turn to Justin, and the speaker repeatedly frames the point as his own answer concerning Jesus's unique influence.

components.text: Whether Jesus's later influence changes the comparative probability of a physical resurrection.

response.rationale: The extraordinary influence claim is relevant to the broader case but does not supply the likelihood bridge needed to answer the prior comparative-probability objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant nonanswer: historical influence is issue-bearing, yet it does not contact the decisive evidential comparison about resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anomaly claim is clear, but uniqueness across all humans and the inference to resurrection lack bounded comparison classes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Worldwide worship is treated as making another extraordinary claim more plausible without a defended causal or probabilistic connection.

charity.alternative: Singular influence may reflect successful belief, institutions, and historical contingencies rather than the truth of a resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: An anomaly in later reception bears on resurrection only through a specific causal or likelihood connection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from one kind of extraordinary outcome to increased probability of a different extraordinary event is a substantial unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Worldwide worship and divine status are observable claims, but their uniqueness and evidential connection to resurrection are not demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the central growth-gap bridge by claiming specific evidential import for Jesus's expansion and status.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notes extraordinariness but materially omits the strongest nonmiraculous explanation of historical influence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass points to billions worshipping Jesus as Lord and God and calls this a singular historical anomaly relevant to resurrection.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The number of people convinced that a miracle occurred establishes widespread belief but not the miracle, because movements acquire adherents for nonmiraculous reasons.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage states the skeptical distinction between proving belief and proving divine intervention, matching Ehrman's immediately preceding objections.

components.text: Whether widespread acceptance or extraordinary influence establishes the miracle believed by adherents.
Whether subsequent Christian spread contributes independently to the cumulative resurrection inference.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the inference's failure by distinguishing evidence that people believed a miracle from evidence that the miracle occurred and names alternative causes of conviction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly targets the decisive inference and states the defeating consequence for both influence and cumulative spread.

precisionFindings.rationale: Belief, truth, miracle, and nonmiraculous causes of adherence are cleanly distinguished without scope drift.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical logical point is calibrated: adherent numbers alone establish conviction, not the event that conviction concerns.

charity.alternative: Unusual scale may be circumstantial evidence if resurrection specifically caused and predicted the movement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Scale alone remains nondiscriminating unless that causal connection is independently established against other growth mechanisms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The separation of widespread belief from the truth of its miraculous object is explicit and defeats the stated popularity-to-miracle inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general existence of nonmiraculous causes of mass conviction strongly supports the bounded claim, though examples are omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central growth-gap bridge separating religious expansion from Jesus's physical fate.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest circumstantial reading while preserving the decisive distinction between belief and occurrence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues that numbers convinced show only that people were convinced and notes that movements gain adherents for other reasons.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: The proposed evidence is not popularity alone but the improbable fulfillment of the specific worldwide mission attributed to the risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly corrects the preceding characterization, develops Bass's Moroni comparison, and returns to Jesus's worldwide mission.

components.text: Whether the argument relies merely on popularity or on fulfillment of a specific mission prediction.
Whether specific mission fulfillment materially changes resurrection's comparative probability.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing raw popularity with specific predicted mission fulfillment, preserving the legitimate evidential issue, though it does not establish comparative likelihood.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe directly corrects the target and answers the replacement demand, but leaves attribution, specificity, and rival fulfillment mechanisms open.

precisionFindings.rationale: The prediction-fulfillment proposition is clear, but 'all nations' and fulfillment after two millennia lack explicit scope criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bass presents fulfillment as some evidence rather than proof, but the improbability and resurrection-specificity remain underqualified.

charity.alternative: A later-attributed broad mission can be fulfilled through ordinary institutional expansion without validating resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its evidential force depends on early attribution, risky specificity, genuine completion, and comparative likelihood under alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Specific risky prediction can be evidence, but the bridge from eventual mission success to physical resurrection remains materially incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A mission saying and broad Christian diffusion are named, while attribution, fulfillment criteria, and improbability are not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central growth-gap bridge by proposing a resurrection-specific mission connection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move improves on a popularity argument but omits several decisive qualifications of the strongest alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass distinguishes popularity from Jesus's attributed claim that the gospel would reach all nations and its alleged later fulfillment.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The worldwide-mission saying comes through later Gospel authors, religious growth does not indicate truth, and incomplete global conversion undercuts the claimed fulfillment.
moves.attributionBasis: Bass directly addresses Bart, and the responding speaker states Ehrman's authorship position and consistently rejects the argument as theological rather than historical.

components.text: Whether a specific saying reliably attributable to Jesus was improbably and fully fulfilled by worldwide expansion.
Whether religious growth is independently indicative of the truth of resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply attacks attribution, denies that growth indicates truth, and contests completion, identifying multiple failures in the mission-fulfillment inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the prediction's source, evidential bridge, and fulfillment condition and states why the conclusion does not follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: Later authorship, growth-versus-truth, and incomplete conversion are distinct, stable objections to the specified claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that this is not a historical resurrection argument is forceful but supported by three expressly stated inferential defects.

charity.alternative: A mission saying could be early, broad proclamation could count as fulfillment, and such fulfillment could be circumstantial evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even that reading requires reliable attribution and a discriminating connection between ordinary expansion and physical resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Each objection independently weakens the inference, and together they explicitly defeat its attribution, fulfillment, and relevance bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Later Gospel mediation, incomplete worldwide conversion, and generic religious growth provide specific support, though detailed dating is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central growth-gap bridge against the mission-fulfillment argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest prediction reading through attribution, completion, and evidential-specificity qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman attributes the saying to later Gospel authors, rejects growth as a truth indicator, and disputes full worldwide fulfillment.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Reports of Jesus appearing in dreams and visions across cultures and centuries are offered as additional evidence that he rose and remains active.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests another argument from Justin, and the speaker identifies his own Jordan experience and forthcoming book before presenting it.

response.rationale: This is the constructive introduction of the later-visions line and therefore has no earlier opposing locked demand to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly identifies the phenomenon and claimed inference, but representative verification is limited.

precisionFindings.rationale: Dreams and visions are grouped together, and claims covering nearly every nation and two millennia lack defined scope and verification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The worldwide reports are called evidence of continuing activity without adequate qualification about ordinary dreaming or selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Continuing agency could predict visions, but reports of dreams and visions do not without further bridge establish their external source.
